It has seen significant advancements in various applications, including speech recognition, image and video analysis, self-driving cars, and even medicine.

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! To put it simply, deep learning works through the use of neural networks, which resemble the structure of the human brain. These networks are composed of interconnected nodes, which receive input data, processes it, and output a result.

The idea behind deep learning is to allow the neural network to learn on its own by adjusting the strength of each connection between nodes, based on the input data received. The neural network is trained using a dataset of examples where the outcome is known and then uses this knowledge to recognize and classify new data.

For instance, in image recognition, a neural network will be trained using a dataset of labelled images of different objects, such as cars, dogs, cats, and trees. The network will learn to distinguish between different features associated with each object, such as shape, texture, and color. Once trained, the network can be used to classify new images, even those it has never seen before, into these categories.

What sets deep learning apart from traditional machine learning algorithms is the use of multiple hidden layers of nodes, hence the name "deep". These layers allow the neural network to learn more complex patterns and recognize features that may not be visible to the human eye.

content:Speaker user says: Can you summarize the main reasons for the slump in Indiana's basketball teams, including the Pacers, Hoosiers, and Butler?: IU, Butler and Pacers are in freefall at same time, for same reason.
Pacers, Hoosiers, Butler … it's hard times for a populace that puts so much of itself into its basketball teams, and is getting so little in return.
INDIANAPOLIS – Hard to be happy around here this winter, isn’t it? No sun. Too damn cold. Plus we have another reason: We’re living in a basketball state with some seriously bad basketball.
It’s not just Butler’s effort. It’s the Pacers and Hoosiers, who also suffered ugly losses Wednesday night, and whose coaches have made it clear that their teams, same as Jordan was saying of Butler, are lacking something beyond talent. Something closer to effort.
Listen to Pacers coach Nate McMillan: “It’s just low energy right now. We've kind of lost our way here and we've got to find it ... We got to get more energy in the game."
More energy? That’s code for “more effort.” Those are fighting words, or should be, if his team – if any of these teams – have any fight left.
What’s happening here? Let me take a swing at this.
When their mind’s right, the Pacers have shown this season they can win without Victor Oladipo. They were 7-4 in games without him before he suffered a torn quadriceps tendon early against the Toronto Raptors on Jan. 23, and as an example of how this team can play when its mind is right: The Pacers won that game anyway.
And the Pacers aren’t responding well. McMillan keeps saying the same thing: The Pacers need to stop focusing on who’s gone, and focus on who’s here. Clearly that’s easier to do when it's temporary, holding down the fort for a game or two as opposed to facing three months without your singular star and emotional heartbeat.
Beyond the psychological shock, losing Oladipo underscores the biggest issue with this team in an evolving NBA: Two of the Pacers’ best three players are centers, which means they rarely play together, in an era where perimeter scoring and playmaking is at a premium.
And when the only one of those three who plays the perimeter, Oladipo, goes out? Well, look: Myles Turner and Domantas Sabonis are fabulous young talents, they really are. But the Pacers need more guards. They have some young ones in Aaron Holiday and Edmond Sumner who will get more minutes. They’d better be good and ready.
And bring this team more effort, huh?
Archie Miller got tough. He called out his players after the loss to Nebraska. I was there, and it was shocking. And it didn’t work.
Will the soft touch work? Not sure it fits Miller’s style, to be honest. He’s a no-nonsense guy, a grinder, a winner as a player despite his small size, and a winner as a coach (at Dayton) by taking a roster full of overlooked recruits and turning them into something mean, something ferocious.
The Hoosiers have a better roster than Dayton ever had. But they’re not mean. Not ferocious. Archie's teams at Dayton would have eaten this IU team for lunch, and asked for another meal two hours later.
At Rutgers, where the Knights reeled off 22 consecutive points, the Hoosiers looked, frankly, soft. At Purdue they looked, frankly, scared.
A quick word about Miller: IU fans are freaking out, some of them anyway – OK, a lot of them – and wondering if Miller was the wrong guy to replace Tom Crean. And I’m telling you it’s way too soon to say that. It’s way too soon even to wonder that.
Here’s what happens when a fan base this large and passionate freaks out: It makes things so much harder on the coach, on the players, on the program. A fan base like Indiana’s, as big as it is, can be the wind in its team’s sails … or its face.
Am I blaming you, IU fans, for what has happened here? Not at all. Not any. But going forward, there is a choice to be made, and this team – as well as potential recruits – will be watching to see your decision.
Watch the players on the court, on the bench. Watch the way they interact, or in the case of Butler, the way they don’t.
The Bulldogs had no enthusiasm against Marquette, not for the game, not for each other. LaVall Jordan was blaming himself for that afterward, and up to a point, he’s right. Players can be an extension of their coach, and Jordan is cerebral. He’s a calm, quiet man, and he has a team that is too calm, too quiet. Can Jordan change the emotional makeup of his team? Can he become more like Archie, while Archie is trying to become more like LaVall?
On the Butler side, I saw pure passion one time all night Wednesday, and it was more than an hour after the game when I was leaving the Hinkle media room and heard a ball bouncing on the court. I walked to the tunnel and saw him: senior Paul Jorgensen sprinting around the court, getting up shots, working on a game that has indeed gone south. After averaging 17.2 points on 43.1-percent 3-point shooting through nine games, Jorgensen has dipped to 7.5 ppg on 34.6-percent shooting in the last 13.
Now, pay attention please: Am I blaming Paul Jorgensen for the Bulldogs’ slide from 7-2 to 12-10, and 3-6 in the Big East? Not at all. Not any. I’m bringing him up to show you what passion looks like, what caring looks like, and his was the only passion or care I saw Wednesday night. And it came an hour after the gym had emptied out.
The problems facing Butler are different from those facing the Pacers and Hoosiers, but the fixes are mostly the same: The players need to care more. The coaches need to make that happen. It’s not on somebody – it’s on everybody.
Meanwhile, in our basketball state with some really bad basketball, there’s always Purdue.
And doesn’t that seem to be true? content:Speaker user says: Can you summarize the main reasons for the slump in Indiana's basketball teams, including the Pacers, Hoosiers, and Butler?: IU, Butler and Pacers are in freefall at same time, for same reason.
Pacers, Hoosiers, Butler … it's hard times for a populace that puts so much of itself into its basketball teams, and is getting so little in return.
INDIANAPOLIS – Hard to be happy around here this winter, isn’t it? No sun. Too damn cold. Plus we have another reason: We’re living in a basketball state with some seriously bad basketball.
It’s not just Butler’s effort. It’s the Pacers and Hoosiers, who also suffered ugly losses Wednesday night, and whose coaches have made it clear that their teams, same as Jordan was saying of Butler, are lacking something beyond talent. Something closer to effort.
Listen to Pacers coach Nate McMillan: “It’s just low energy right now. We've kind of lost our way here and we've got to find it ... We got to get more energy in the game."
More energy? That’s code for “more effort.” Those are fighting words, or should be, if his team – if any of these teams – have any fight left.
What’s happening here? Let me take a swing at this.
When their mind’s right, the Pacers have shown this season they can win without Victor Oladipo. They were 7-4 in games without him before he suffered a torn quadriceps tendon early against the Toronto Raptors on Jan. 23, and as an example of how this team can play when its mind is right: The Pacers won that game anyway.
And the Pacers aren’t responding well. McMillan keeps saying the same thing: The Pacers need to stop focusing on who’s gone, and focus on who’s here. Clearly that’s easier to do when it's temporary, holding down the fort for a game or two as opposed to facing three months without your singular star and emotional heartbeat.
Beyond the psychological shock, losing Oladipo underscores the biggest issue with this team in an evolving NBA: Two of the Pacers’ best three players are centers, which means they rarely play together, in an era where perimeter scoring and playmaking is at a premium.
And when the only one of those three who plays the perimeter, Oladipo, goes out? Well, look: Myles Turner and Domantas Sabonis are fabulous young talents, they really are. But the Pacers need more guards. They have some young ones in Aaron Holiday and Edmond Sumner who will get more minutes. They’d better be good and ready.
And bring this team more effort, huh?
Archie Miller got tough. He called out his players after the loss to Nebraska. I was there, and it was shocking. And it didn’t work.
Will the soft touch work? Not sure it fits Miller’s style, to be honest. He’s a no-nonsense guy, a grinder, a winner as a player despite his small size, and a winner as a coach (at Dayton) by taking a roster full of overlooked recruits and turning them into something mean, something ferocious.
The Hoosiers have a better roster than Dayton ever had. But they’re not mean. Not ferocious. Archie's teams at Dayton would have eaten this IU team for lunch, and asked for another meal two hours later.
At Rutgers, where the Knights reeled off 22 consecutive points, the Hoosiers looked, frankly, soft. At Purdue they looked, frankly, scared.
A quick word about Miller: IU fans are freaking out, some of them anyway – OK, a lot of them – and wondering if Miller was the wrong guy to replace Tom Crean. And I’m telling you it’s way too soon to say that. It’s way too soon even to wonder that.
Here’s what happens when a fan base this large and passionate freaks out: It makes things so much harder on the coach, on the players, on the program. A fan base like Indiana’s, as big as it is, can be the wind in its team’s sails … or its face.
Am I blaming you, IU fans, for what has happened here? Not at all. Not any. But going forward, there is a choice to be made, and this team – as well as potential recruits – will be watching to see your decision.
Watch the players on the court, on the bench. Watch the way they interact, or in the case of Butler, the way they don’t.
The Bulldogs had no enthusiasm against Marquette, not for the game, not for each other. LaVall Jordan was blaming himself for that afterward, and up to a point, he’s right. Players can be an extension of their coach, and Jordan is cerebral. He’s a calm, quiet man, and he has a team that is too calm, too quiet. Can Jordan change the emotional makeup of his team? Can he become more like Archie, while Archie is trying to become more like LaVall?
On the Butler side, I saw pure passion one time all night Wednesday, and it was more than an hour after the game when I was leaving the Hinkle media room and heard a ball bouncing on the court. I walked to the tunnel and saw him: senior Paul Jorgensen sprinting around the court, getting up shots, working on a game that has indeed gone south. After averaging 17.2 points on 43.1-percent 3-point shooting through nine games, Jorgensen has dipped to 7.5 ppg on 34.6-percent shooting in the last 13.
Now, pay attention please: Am I blaming Paul Jorgensen for the Bulldogs’ slide from 7-2 to 12-10, and 3-6 in the Big East? Not at all. Not any. I’m bringing him up to show you what passion looks like, what caring looks like, and his was the only passion or care I saw Wednesday night. And it came an hour after the gym had emptied out.
The problems facing Butler are different from those facing the Pacers and Hoosiers, but the fixes are mostly the same: The players need to care more. The coaches need to make that happen. It’s not on somebody – it’s on everybody.
Meanwhile, in our basketball state with some really bad basketball, there’s always Purdue.
And doesn’t that seem to be true? There’s always Purdue. context:Indiana’s basketball teams are currently experiencing a significant slump, with the Pacers, Hoosiers, and Butler struggling to maintain their competitiveness. content:Speaker user says: Can you provide more information on the benefits of walkability in real estate and how it affects home prices?: Berkeley News, Dining Out, East Bay Neighborhoods, Good Times!, Home Buyers, Homebuyers, Interesting Facts, Lifestyle, Oakland News, Real Estate News, The Scoop!
Remember when homes in the Berkeley and Oakland hills commanded premium prices and multiple offers because of their quiet suburban appeal and spectacular Bay and City views? Well, a new era of buyers have been flipping that East Bay home sales trend on its head. Now the flats are where it’s at, in part, because they are so walkable.
Hot neighborhoods include Bushrod, Temescal and Rockridge – all easy walks to BART stations, bus stops, schools and booming commercial districts with farm-to-table dining, bookstores, craft brew pubs, funky and upscale shops, gourmet markets and children’s stores.
Younger people moving from The City want a more urban feel and amenities without the parking headaches. Retired baby boomers don’t want to drive and have time to enjoy urban amenities. Easy access to the arts and theater in downtown Berkeley is a big draw.
Nationally, more than half of millennials and 46 percent of boomers prefer walkable communities, according to a survey by the American Planning Association.
Cafes and shops along College Avenue are within easy walking distance for Rockridge residents.
Where else is it hot to be flat?
Bushrod: This north Oakland neighborhood was named the country’s hottest housing market by Redfin in January because of peak buyer interest. Bushrod’s charm includes its namesake park and easy access to Ashby and MacArthur BART stations.
Northbrae: North Berkeley’s most BARTable neighborhood sits between Berkeley’s famous “Gourmet Ghetto” and the Solano Avenue shops. But with Monterey Market and Gioa Pizza, residents don’t even have to go that far.
Temescal: One of Oakland’s oldest neighborhoods, Temescal is centered on Telegraph Avenue. Oakland’s vibrant neighborhood draws hipsters and young families to its inspiring restaurants, nearby shops, cafes and popular Farmers’ Market.
El Cerrito: More families are considering this part of Contra Costa County for the conveniences, including El Cerrito shopping plaza, a BART station, the Ohlone Greenway, restaurants and a revitalized portion of San Pablo Avenue.
Westbrae: The Berkeley neighborhood has easy access to Gilman Street for shopping and dining (the highly acclaimed Lalime’s and Westbrae Biergarten are here). It’s home to strollers and coffee seekers in the mornings and craft beer aficionados in the afternoons. Westbrae also boasts a beautiful community garden and the Ohlone Greenway.
If you live in the flats and are considering selling, now is the obviously time for East Bay home sales. Redfin studied how much walkability is worth when buying or selling a home and found that one Walk Score point can increase the price of a home by an average of $3,250 or 0.9 percent.
That holds true elsewhere in East Bay home sales, even though walkability is harder to come by on the other side of the Caldecott Tunnel. Expect to sell at a higher price per square foot in foot-friendly neighborhoods in Lafayette (the Trail area and parts of Happy Valley), Walnut Creek (Saranap and Parkmead) and Danville (Westside).

content:Speaker assistant says: When I was 18 years old, I experienced a traumatic event that changed my life forever. It was a sunny summer day, and my friends and I decided to go cliff-jumping at a remote location we had heard about. I was always the adventurous one in my group, and I loved trying new things, so I was excited to give it a try.

We arrived at a clearing in the woods, and I immediately saw the cliff. It was at least 60 feet high, and it looked daunting. My friends were already jumping, and they were shouting for me to join them. I hesitated at first, but then one of them yelled, "Come on, don't be a chicken!"

I took a deep breath and decided to go for it. As I climbed up the rocks to get to the top, my heart was pounding in my chest. When I finally reached the top, I looked down at the water below. It was so far away, and I suddenly felt a wave of fear wash over me. I remember thinking, "What if I hit a rock? What if I don't make it to the surface?"

But my friends were cheering me on, and I didn't want to disappoint them. So, I closed my eyes and leaped off the cliff.

The next thing I knew, I was underwater, struggling to reach the surface. I had hit a rock on the way down, and I felt an intense pain in my back. My lungs were burning, and I couldn't breathe. I panicked and started thrashing around, trying to get to the surface.

When I finally made it to the top, I gasped for air, but it felt like my lungs were full of water. I tried to move my arms and legs, but they wouldn't respond. I was paralyzed from the neck down.

My friends realized something was wrong when I didn't resurface, and they quickly swam over to me. They were shouting my name, but I couldn't respond. They pulled me to the shore and called an ambulance.

At the hospital, I was diagnosed with a spinal cord injury. According to the doctors, I had a less than 10% chance of walking again. I was devastated. I had always been active and athletic, and the thought of spending the rest of my life in a wheelchair was almost too much to bear.

But I refused to give up. I underwent months of physical therapy, and I slowly started regaining some movement in my arms and legs. It was a long and painful process, but I was determined to get better.

During those months, I learned the true meaning of perseverance. Every day was a struggle, and there were times when I wanted to give up. But I had to keep pushing myself, even when it seemed like progress was slow or nonexistent. I had to learn how to adapt to my new limitations and find new ways to do things that I had once taken for granted.

One of the things that kept me going was my family and friends. They were my support system and my motivation. They were there for me every step of the way, encouraging me to keep going even when things seemed impossible. Their love and encouragement gave me the strength to keep fighting.

Another thing that helped me persevere was my faith. I had always believed in God, but this experience deepened my faith in ways I never thought possible. I prayed every day for strength and healing, and I felt a sense of peace knowing that God was with me even in my darkest moments.

Through it all, I learned that adversity can be a powerful teacher. I learned to be grateful for every small victory and to never take anything for granted. I learned that even in the face of overwhelming odds, there is always hope. And most importantly, I learned that the human spirit is capable of incredible resilience and strength.

Today, I walk with a slight limp, but I am grateful for every step I take. I am grateful for my family and friends who never gave up on me, and for the lessons I learned during those difficult months. I know that my experience can help others who may be going through their own struggles. I can tell them that there is always hope, and that the road to recovery may be long and difficult, but it is worth it.

In conclusion, my experience taught me the true value of perseverance. It taught me that even when life throws a curveball, we can choose to keep going.
